claim: Pathogenic fungi cause 2.5 million annually attributable deaths worldwide.
source: Pathogenic fungi are a significant burden to public health, recently estimated to cause 2.5 million annually attributable deaths worldwide (Denning, 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Denning, 2024

claim: Candida species are responsible for more than 100 million mucosal infections and 1.5 million systemic infections.
source: Among these, Candida species are responsible for more than 100 million mucosal infections and 1.5 million systemic infections, representing the fourth most frequent cause of bloodstream infection in hospitalized patients (Denning, 2024; Brown et al., 2012; Sharma and Chakrabarti, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Denning, 2024; Brown et al., 2012; Sharma and Chakrabarti, 2023

claim: Candida species represent the fourth most frequent cause of bloodstream infection in hospitalized patients.
source: Among these, Candida species are responsible for more than 100 million mucosal infections and 1.5 million systemic infections, representing the fourth most frequent cause of bloodstream infection in hospitalized patients (Denning, 2024; Brown et al., 2012; Sharma and Chakrabarti, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Denning, 2024; Brown et al., 2012; Sharma and Chakrabarti, 2023

claim: Candida albicans is the most common opportunistic species.
source: Candida albicans is the most common opportunistic species, which in healthy individuals often colonizes mucosal surfaces (oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, as well as genital tract) (d'Enfert et al., 2021), but leads to invasive infection, post trauma or when immune system of the host is compromised.
evidence: Supported by citation to d'Enfert et al., 2021

claim: C. albicans in healthy individuals often colonizes mucosal surfaces including oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and genital tract.
source: Candida albicans is the most common opportunistic species, which in healthy individuals often colonizes mucosal surfaces (oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, as well as genital tract) (d'Enfert et al., 2021), but leads to invasive infection, post trauma or when immune system of the host is compromised.
evidence: Supported by citation to d'Enfert et al., 2021

claim: C. albicans leads to invasive infection post trauma or when the immune system of the host is compromised.
source: Candida albicans is the most common opportunistic species, which in healthy individuals often colonizes mucosal surfaces (oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, as well as genital tract) (d'Enfert et al., 2021), but leads to invasive infection, post trauma or when immune system of the host is compromised.
evidence: Supported by citation to d'Enfert et al., 2021 and established knowledge of opportunistic infections

claim: C. albicans is classified in the critical priority group of the WHO list of fungal pathogens.
source: C. albicans is classified in the critical priority group of the WHO list of fungal pathogens (WHO, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2022

claim: The fungal cell wall is essential for protection, integrity, and to maintain cell morphology.
source: Fungal cells are enveloped by a cell wall, which is essential for protection, integrity, and to maintain cell morphology.
evidence: Established knowledge about fungal cell wall function

claim: During commensalism with human hosts, the cell wall enables fungi to survive host defenses.
source: During commensalism with human hosts, the cell wall enables fungi to survive host defenses, whereas during pathogenic interactions the cell wall also plays a central role in the polarized growth of invasive hyphae, thereby facilitating host tissue invasion (Hall, 2015; Mishra et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall, 2015; Mishra et al., 2022

claim: During pathogenic interactions the cell wall plays a central role in the polarized growth of invasive hyphae, thereby facilitating host tissue invasion.
source: During commensalism with human hosts, the cell wall enables fungi to survive host defenses, whereas during pathogenic interactions the cell wall also plays a central role in the polarized growth of invasive hyphae, thereby facilitating host tissue invasion (Hall, 2015; Mishra et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall, 2015; Mishra et al., 2022

claim: The cell wall architecture is dynamic and critical in modulating the host immune responses.
source: The cell wall architecture is dynamic and therefore critical in modulating the host immune responses (Brown, 2011; Netea et al., 2015), which are driven by host immune receptors (pattern recognition receptors [PRRs]) (Netea et al., 2006; Erwig and Gow, 2016; Dambuza et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown, 2011; Netea et al., 2015; Netea et al., 2006; Erwig and Gow, 2016; Dambuza et al., 2017

claim: Host immune responses are driven by host immune receptors (pattern recognition receptors [PRRs]).
source: The cell wall architecture is dynamic and therefore critical in modulating the host immune responses (Brown, 2011; Netea et al., 2015), which are driven by host immune receptors (pattern recognition receptors [PRRs]) (Netea et al., 2006; Erwig and Gow, 2016; Dambuza et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Netea et al., 2006; Erwig and Gow, 2016; Dambuza et al., 2017

claim: Recognition of fungal pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by host PRRs triggers an array of antifungal responses, including phagocytosis, the production of reactive oxygen/nitrogen species (ROS/RNS), neutrophil extracellular traps, and the release of cytokines and chemokines.
source: Recognition of fungal pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) by host PRRs triggers an array of antifungal responses, including phagocytosis, the production of reactive oxygen/nitrogen species (ROS/RNS), neutrophil extracellular traps, and the release of cytokines and chemokines that recruit immune cells to the site of infection and activate adaptive immunity (Dambuza et al., 2017; Lionakis and Levitz, 2018; Urban et al., 2006; Gow et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dambuza et al., 2017; Lionakis and Levitz, 2018; Urban et al., 2006; Gow et al., 2011

claim: Fungal cell wall components function as the major PAMPs.
source: Being extracellular, thereby first to interact with the host immune system, fungal cell wall components function as the major PAMPs.
evidence: Logical inference from the extracellular location of cell wall components and their role in immune recognition

claim: The cell wall of C. albicans is a complex structure with a fibrillar outer layer of mannoproteins and an inner polysaccharide layer composed of chitin, β-1,3-glucan and β-1,6-glucan.
source: The cell wall of C. albicans is a complex structure with a fibrillar outer layer of mannoproteins and an inner polysaccharide layer composed of chitin, β-1,3-glucan and β-1,6-glucan, which are not present in mammalian cells (Gow and Hube, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gow and Hube, 2012

claim: Chitin, β-1,3-glucan and β-1,6-glucan are not present in mammalian cells.
source: The cell wall of C. albicans is a complex structure with a fibrillar outer layer of mannoproteins and an inner polysaccharide layer composed of chitin, β-1,3-glucan and β-1,6-glucan, which are not present in mammalian cells (Gow and Hube, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gow and Hube, 2012 and established knowledge

claim: Dectin-1, a C-type lectin receptor that recognizes fungal cell wall β-1,3-glucan, has been demonstrated to play a dominant pro-inflammatory role in antifungal immunity.
source: Dectin-1, a C-type lectin receptor that recognizes fungal cell wall β-1,3-glucan, has been demonstrated to play a dominant pro-inflammatory role in antifungal immunity (Brown et al., 2002; Brown and Gordon, 2003; Taylor et al., 2007; Ferwerda et al., 2009; Marakalala et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 2002; Brown and Gordon, 2003; Taylor et al., 2007; Ferwerda et al., 2009; Marakalala et al., 2013

claim: Chitin particles derived from the C. albicans cell wall lead to the selective secretion of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.
source: Chitin particles derived from the C. albicans cell wall lead to the selective secretion of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 (Wagener et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wagener et al., 2014

claim: Mannans from C. albicans are recognized by multiple receptors expressed on different immune cells (Mannose receptor, DC-SIGN, TLR4, Dectin-2, Dectin-3).
source: Mannans from C. albicans are recognized by multiple receptors expressed on different immune cells (Mannose receptor, DC-SIGN, TLR4, Dectin-2, Dectin-3), which are involved in yeast phagocytosis and appear to play a critical role in the induction of Th17 responses (Hall and Gow, 2013; Choudhury et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall and Gow, 2013; Choudhury et al., 2023

claim: Mannan receptors are involved in yeast phagocytosis and appear to play a critical role in the induction of Th17 responses.
source: Mannans from C. albicans are recognized by multiple receptors expressed on different immune cells (Mannose receptor, DC-SIGN, TLR4, Dectin-2, Dectin-3), which are involved in yeast phagocytosis and appear to play a critical role in the induction of Th17 responses (Hall and Gow, 2013; Choudhury et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hall and Gow, 2013; Choudhury et al., 2023

claim: Low levels of β-1,3-glucan exposure by C. albicans correlate with enhanced colonization of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: For example, low levels of β-1,3-glucan exposure by C. albicans correlate with enhanced colonization of the gastrointestinal tract (Sem et al., 2016; Hopke et al., 2018) and β-1,3-glucan is mainly hidden from immune recognition by the outer layer of mannan fibrils (Erwig and Gow, 2016; Lenardon et al., 2020; Graus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sem et al., 2016; Hopke et al., 2018

claim: β-1,3-glucan is mainly hidden from immune recognition by the outer layer of mannan fibrils.
source: For example, low levels of β-1,3-glucan exposure by C. albicans correlate with enhanced colonization of the gastrointestinal tract (Sem et al., 2016; Hopke et al., 2018) and β-1,3-glucan is mainly hidden from immune recognition by the outer layer of mannan fibrils (Erwig and Gow, 2016; Lenardon et al., 2020; Graus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erwig and Gow, 2016; Lenardon et al., 2020; Graus et al., 2018

claim: β-Glucans and chitin account for about 60% and 2–10% (depending on the morphotype), respectively, of the C. albicans cell wall.
source: β-Glucans and chitin, which account for about 60% and 2–10% (depending on the morphotype), respectively, are cross-linked to form the skeletal armor of the C. albicans cell wall (Gow et al., 2011; Klis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gow et al., 2011; Klis et al., 2009

claim: β-Glucans and chitin are cross-linked to form the skeletal armor of the C. albicans cell wall.
source: β-Glucans and chitin, which account for about 60% and 2–10% (depending on the morphotype), respectively, are cross-linked to form the skeletal armor of the C. albicans cell wall (Gow et al., 2011; Klis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gow et al., 2011; Klis et al., 2009

claim: Mannoproteins account for 30–40% of the cell wall.
source: Mannoproteins, which are predominantly glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-modified and covalently linked to the skeletal polysaccharides via β-1,6-glucan bridges (Klis et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016), account for 30–40% of the cell wall.
evidence: Supported by citations to Klis et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016

claim: Mannoproteins are predominantly glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-modified and covalently linked to the skeletal polysaccharides via β-1,6-glucan bridges.
source: Mannoproteins, which are predominantly glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-modified and covalently linked to the skeletal polysaccharides via β-1,6-glucan bridges (Klis et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016), account for 30–40% of the cell wall.
evidence: Supported by citations to Klis et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2016

claim: β-1,6-Glucan is composed of a linear chain of β-1,6-linked glucose residues with few short side chains of β-1,3-glucoside or laminaribioside residues.
source: β-1,6-Glucan is composed of a linear chain of β-1,6-linked glucose residues with few short side chains of β-1,3-glucoside or laminaribioside residues (Iorio et al., 2008; Aimanianda et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iorio et al., 2008; Aimanianda et al., 2009

claim: According to analytical methods, the β-1,6-glucan content is highly variable, from 15 to 50%.
source: According to analytical methods, the β-1,6-glucan content is highly variable, from 15 to 50% (Mio et al., 1997; Herrero et al., 2004; Free, 2013; Schiavone et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mio et al., 1997; Herrero et al., 2004; Free, 2013; Schiavone et al., 2014

claim: KRE5 codes a putative α-glucosyltransferase (GT-24) localized in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Among them, KRE5 codes a putative α-glucosyltransferase (CAZy, 2024a) (GT-24) localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); its deletion results in the absence of β-1,6-glucan in S. cerevisiae and about 80% reduction in cell wall β-1,6-glucan content in C. albicans (Herrero et al., 2004; Levinson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to CAZy, 2024a; Herrero et al., 2004; Levinson et al., 2002

claim: Deletion of KRE5 results in the absence of β-1,6-glucan in S. cerevisiae and about 80% reduction in cell wall β-1,6-glucan content in C. albicans.
source: Among them, KRE5 codes a putative α-glucosyltransferase (CAZy, 2024a) (GT-24) localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); its deletion results in the absence of β-1,6-glucan in S. cerevisiae and about 80% reduction in cell wall β-1,6-glucan content in C. albicans (Herrero et al., 2004; Levinson et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herrero et al., 2004; Levinson et al., 2002

claim: KRE6 and its functional homolog SKN1 share 66% identity and both encode transmembrane proteins containing a glycosyl-hydrolase domain (GH-16).
source: KRE6 and its functional homolog SKN1 share 66% identity and both encode transmembrane proteins containing a glycosyl-hydrolase domain (GH-16).
evidence: Established knowledge about protein structure and sequence similarity

claim: KRE6 deletion in S. cerevisiae results in a 70% decrease in the cell wall β-1,6-glucan content.
source: KRE6 deletion in S. cerevisiae results in a 70% decrease in the cell wall β-1,6-glucan content (Aimanianda et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aimanianda et al., 2009

claim: In C. albicans, the double deletion of KRE6 and SKN1 leads to a slow growth, cell wall abnormalities, cell separation failure, and reduced virulence.
source: In C. albicans, the double deletion of KRE6 and SKN1 leads to a slow growth, cell wall abnormalities, cell separation failure, and reduced virulence (Han et al., 2019a; Han et al., 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2019a; Han et al., 2019b

claim: The C. albicans cell wall is composed of 3% of chitin, 43% of proteins/mannoproteins (27% of mannans), and 54% of β-glucans.
source: Overall, we found that the C. albicans cell wall is composed of 3% of chitin, 43% of proteins/mannoproteins (27% of mannans), and 54% of β-glucans, which was in agreement with earlier studies and validated our analytic approach (Figure 1a and b; Chaffin et al., 1998; Garcia-Rubio et al., 2020; Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1a and b and citations to Chaffin et al., 1998; Garcia-Rubio et al., 2020; Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006

claim: In SD medium at 37°C, β-1,6-glucan represents 23% of the total cell wall, with an average size of 58 kDa.
source: In SD medium at 37°C, β-1,6-glucan represents 23% of the total cell wall, with an average size of 58 kDa (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1

claim: An average of 6.4% (± 0.5%) of glucose units of the main chain are substituted by a single glucose residue (88–90%) or a laminaribiose (10–12%).
source: According to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis and high-performance anion exchange chromatography (HPAEC) after endo-β-1,6-glucanase digestion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), based on three independent experiments, an average of 6.4% (± 0.5%) of glucose units of the main chain are substituted by a single glucose residue (88–90%) or a laminaribiose (10–12%).
evidence: Supported by NMR and HPAEC data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: β-1,6-glucan corresponded to 23% of the total cell wall and was mainly found in the AI fraction.
source: β-1,6-Glucan corresponded to 23% of the total cell wall and was mainly found in the AI fraction (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1a and b

claim: β-1,6-glucan in the AI fraction could be solubilized by digesting β-1,3-glucan using an endo-β-1,3-glucanase, confirming that it is covalently linked to the cell wall β-1,3-glucan.
source: β-1,6-Glucan in the AI fraction could be solubilized by digesting β-1,3-glucan using an endo-β-1,3-glucanase, confirming that it is covalently linked to the cell wall β-1,3-glucan as previously shown in S. cerevisiae (Aimanianda et al., 2009; Kollár et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citations to Aimanianda et al., 2009; Kollár et al., 1997

claim: The solubilized β-1,6-glucan was eluted in a single symmetric peak with Gaussian shape showing a homogeneous polymer with an apparent molecular weight range of 18–112 kDa.
source: Further, gel filtration chromatography showed that the solubilized β-1,6-glucan was eluted in a single symmetric peak with Gaussian shape showing a homogeneous polymer with an apparent molecular weight range of 18–112 kDa (Figure 1d), and the average molecular weight was estimated to be 58 kDa.
evidence: Supported by gel filtration data in Figure 1d

claim: The average molecular weight of β-1,6-glucan was estimated to be 58 kDa.
source: Further, gel filtration chromatography showed that the solubilized β-1,6-glucan was eluted in a single symmetric peak with Gaussian shape showing a homogeneous polymer with an apparent molecular weight range of 18–112 kDa (Figure 1d), and the average molecular weight was estimated to be 58 kDa.
evidence: Supported by gel filtration data in Figure 1d

claim: β-1,6-glucan is a major cell wall polymer in C. albicans, representing 40% of the cell wall β-glucans.
source: Altogether, our data showed that β-1,6-glucan is a major cell wall polymer in C. albicans, representing 40% of the cell wall β-glucans.
evidence: Inference from the quantitative data presented

claim: No significant difference was observed between cell wall β-1,6-glucan and other polymers produced during the exponential and stationary phases in yeast cells.
source: No significant difference was observed between cell wall β-1,6-glucan and other polymers produced during the exponential (control) and stationary phases in yeast cells (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2

claim: In biofilms, only a slight increase in mannan content (26% vs. 20%), but no change in relative β-glucan content, was observed.
source: In biofilms, only a slight increase in mannan content (26% vs. 20%), but no change in relative β-glucan content, was observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The cell wall isolated from C. albicans hyphae was characterized by an increase in chitin content (10% vs. 3%).
source: In contrast, the cell wall isolated from C. albicans hyphae was characterized by an increase in chitin content (10% vs. 3%) as previously shown (Gow et al., 2017; Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006; Braun and Calderone, 1978), as well as a reduction in β-1,6-glucan (18% vs. 23%) and mannan contents (13% vs. 20%) compared to the yeast form.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Gow et al., 2017; Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006; Braun and Calderone, 1978

claim: The cell wall isolated from C. albicans hyphae showed a reduction in β-1,6-glucan (18% vs. 23%) and mannan contents (13% vs. 20%) compared to the yeast form.
source: In contrast, the cell wall isolated from C. albicans hyphae was characterized by an increase in chitin content (10% vs. 3%) as previously shown (Gow et al., 2017; Ruiz-Herrera et al., 2006; Braun and Calderone, 1978), as well as a reduction in β-1,6-glucan (18% vs. 23%) and mannan contents (13% vs. 20%) compared to the yeast form.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The decrease in β-1,6-glucan content in hyphae was reflected in a reduction in the β-1,6-glucan size (43 vs. 58 kDa).
source: The decrease in β-1,6-glucan content was reflected in a reduction in the β-1,6-glucan size (43 vs. 58 kDa), demonstrating that both content and structure of β-1,6-glucan are regulated during growth and cellular morphogenesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Both content and structure of β-1,6-glucan are regulated during growth and cellular morphogenesis.
source: The decrease in β-1,6-glucan content was reflected in a reduction in the β-1,6-glucan size (43 vs. 58 kDa), demonstrating that both content and structure of β-1,6-glucan are regulated during growth and cellular morphogenesis.
evidence: Inference from the observed changes in β-1,6-glucan content and size

claim: A higher branching rate of β-1,3-glucan of the hyphal cell wall was observed in the AI fraction (7.3% vs. 5.3%).
source: In addition, a higher branching rate of β-1,3-glucan of the hyphal cell wall was also observed in the AI fraction (7.3% vs. 5.3%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Growth at 30°C or in 1 M NaCl led to a decrease in the cell wall β-1,6-glucan content and a decrease in β-1,6-glucan chain length.
source: For example, growth at 30°C or in 1 M NaCl led to a decrease in the cell wall β-1,6-glucan content and a decrease in β-1,6-glucan chain length.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Decreases in β-1,6-glucan at low temperature were compensated by a higher content of less-branched β-1,3-glucan.
source: However, these decreases at low temperature were compensated by a higher content of less-branched β-1,3-glucan, whereas high salt led to an increased branching rate of both β-1,6-glucan and β-1,3-glucan (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: High salt led to an increased branching rate of both β-1,6-glucan and β-1,3-glucan.
source: However, these decreases at low temperature were compensated by a higher content of less-branched β-1,3-glucan, whereas high salt led to an increased branching rate of both β-1,6-glucan and β-1,3-glucan (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Buffered culture medium at pH 4 or 7.5 led to a slight decrease in the β-1,6-glucan molecular weight and an increase in its branching frequency in comparison to buffered medium at pH 5.4.
source: Buffered culture medium at pH 4 or 7.5 led to a slight decrease in the β-1,6-glucan molecular weight and an increase in its branching frequency in comparison to buffered medium at pH 5.4.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The most pronounced alteration of the cell wall was observed in lactate containing medium, with a steep reduction in polysaccharides from the structural core, chitin (–43%), β-1,3-glucan (–48%), and mainly β-1,6-glucan (–72%).
source: However, the most pronounced alteration of the cell wall was observed in lactate containing medium, with a steep reduction in polysaccharides from the structural core, chitin (–43%), β-1,3-glucan (–48%), and mainly β-1,6-glucan (–72%), in agreement with the decrease in thickness of the inner cell wall layer previously described (Ene et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Ene et al., 2012

claim: Lactate medium led to a strong reduction in the average β-1,6-glucan molecular weight (19 vs. 58 kDa), a decrease in β-1,6-glucan branching (4.9 vs. 6.4%), and an increase in β-1,3-glucan branching (7.4 vs. 5.3%).
source: Lactate medium also led to a strong reduction in the average β-1,6-glucan molecular weight (19 vs. 58 kDa), a decrease in β-1,6-glucan branching (4.9 vs. 6.4%), and an increase in β-1,3-glucan branching (7.4 vs. 5.3%, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The presence in the medium of short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, or butyrate) at physiological gut concentrations resulted in a growth defect but did not alter the global cell wall composition.
source: The presence in the medium of short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, or butyrate) at physiological gut concentrations resulted in a growth defect but did not alter the global cell wall composition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Short-chain fatty acids resulted in an increase in β-1,6-glucan molecular weight (64–68 kDa vs. 58 kDa).
source: The main difference was an increase in β-1,6-glucan molecular weight (64–68 kDa vs. 58 kDa) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2b

claim: Cell wall chitin content was reduced in the presence of nikkomycin, a chitin synthesis inhibitor.
source: Cell wall chitin content was reduced in the presence of nikkomycin, a chitin synthesis inhibitor, and increased in the presence of the cell wall-damaging agents Congo Red or caspofungin, as previously observed (Chapman et al., 1992; Roncero and Durán, 1985; Walker et al., 2013), but with no impact on β-1,3-glucan and β-1,6-glucan contents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Chapman et al., 1992; Roncero and Durán, 1985; Walker et al., 2013

claim: Cell wall chitin content increased in the presence of the cell wall-damaging agents Congo Red or caspofungin.
source: Cell wall chitin content was reduced in the presence of nikkomycin, a chitin synthesis inhibitor, and increased in the presence of the cell wall-damaging agents Congo Red or caspofungin, as previously observed (Chapman et al., 1992; Roncero and Durán, 1985; Walker et al., 2013), but with no impact on β-1,3-glucan and β-1,6-glucan contents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Chapman et al., 1992; Roncero and Durán, 1985; Walker et al., 2013

claim: The major stress effect observed was in the presence of caspofungin, which caused an increase in the average molecular weight of β-1,6-glucan (70 vs. 58 kDa).
source: The major stress effect we observed was in the presence of caspofungin, which caused an increase in the average molecular weight of β-1,6-glucan (70 vs. 58 kDa).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The content, size, and branching of β-1,6-glucan in the C. albicans cell wall are regulated by numerous environmental growth and stress conditions.
source: These data demonstrate that the content, size, and branching of β-1,6-glucan in the C. albicans cell wall are regulated by numerous environmental growth and stress conditions.
evidence: Inference from the comprehensive data on environmental effects

claim: In the PMRP1-CHS1/chs1Δ mutant, the cell wall had a 45.7% decrease in mannan content in the AS fraction and a 50% increase in β-1,6-glucan in the AI fraction.
source: In the PMRP1-CHS1/chs1Δ mutant, the cell wall had a 45.7% decrease in mannan content in the AS fraction and a 50% increase in β-1,6-glucan in the AI fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3a

claim: In the chs3Δ/Δ mutant, the low proportion of chitin led to an increase in both β-1,3-glucan (×1.6) and β-1,6-glucan (×1.6) in the AS fraction.

evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The increase in β-glucans in the AS fraction of the chs3Δ/Δ mutant suggests a defect in β-glucans cross-linking in the cell wall polysaccharide core.
source: In the chs3Δ/Δ mutant, the low proportion of chitin led to an increase in both β-1,3-glucan (×1.6) and β-1,6-glucan (×1.6) in the AS fraction (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting a defect in β-glucans cross-linking in the cell wall polysaccharide core.
evidence: Inference from the observed increase in soluble β-glucans

claim: No significant effect of the CHS2 deletion was observed on cell wall chitin content or overall wall composition.
source: Strikingly, no significant effect of the CHS2 deletion was observed on cell wall chitin content or overall wall composition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Deletion of PHR2 led to an increase in β-1,3-glucan content and a cross-linking defect (–31.5% estimated on the ratio β-1,3-glucan content in AS and AI fractions).

evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Deletion of PHR2 led to a reduction in cell wall β-1,6-glucan content in both AI (–58.7%) and AS (–51.3%) fractions and to a reduction in molecular weight and branching of the β-1,6-glucan chains.
source: Concomitantly, deletion of PHR2 led to a reduction in cell wall β-1,6-glucan content in both AI (–58.7%) and AS (–51.3%) fractions and to a reduction in molecular weight and branching of the β-1,6-glucan chains (Figure 3a).

claim: In the phr1Δ/Δ mutant, only a significant increase in the molecular weight of β-1,6-glucan chain was observed (60 vs. 50 kDa).
